reference_title: EM 1110-1-1905, Geotechnical Design of Shallow Foundations on Soils (USACE, 31 July 2025)

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body: [p. 66] The design of shallow foundations requires an understanding of the surface and subsurface characteristics on which the supporting structure is founded. This chapter provides general guidance for site exploration and characterization for structures supported on shallow foundations. More detailed information on geotechnical investigations can be found in EM 1110-1-1804. For design of floodwalls and other hydraulic retaining walls, guidance for site exploration is provided in EM 1110-2-2502.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 4 (Site Exploration), paragraph 4-1, printed p. 66.

sections.title: Geotechnical investigations
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 4 (Site Exploration), paragraph 4-2, printed p. 66.

sections.title: General
sections.body: [p. 66] General. Geotechnical investigations should be implemented at the project site and scaled for the intended structure to obtain the engineering characteristics of the site and characterize the stratigraphy and nature of subsurface materials and their expected behavior under structure loadings. The goal of the investigation is to identify adverse subsurface conditions (if present) that could lead to construction difficulties, excessive maintenance, or possible failure of the foundation/structure. The scope of investigations depends on the nature and complexity of subsurface materials and the size, requirements for, and importance of the structure. An experienced geotechnical engineer who is familiar with the region is required to develop the scope of the investigation.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 4 (Site Exploration), paragraph 4-2a, printed p. 66.

sections.title: Problematic ground
sections.body: [p. 66] Problematic ground. Requirements for site exploration and characterization of problematic ground are not covered in this manual. Some considerations for problematic ground are listed in Chapter 10 of this manual.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 4 (Site Exploration), paragraph 4-2b, printed p. 66.

sections.title: Exploration phases
sections.body: [p. 66] Site investigations can be divided into three major phases: review of available information (such as geologic maps), surface examination, and subsurface exploration. Site explorations should be performed with a basic understanding of the parameters that will be needed for design and the expected geologic variability. In some instances, site conditions will vary significantly from those assumed, based on local knowledge of the regional geology. When this occurs, the exploration plan should be modified to provide more detailed data for design relevant to the unanticipated conditions encountered.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 4 (Site Exploration), paragraph 4-3, printed p. 66.

sections.title: Available information
sections.body: [p. 66] Available information. To better understand site conditions, available information (such as geologic and topographic maps, boring data, site modification records) should be reviewed. These documents can better guide the site exploration and potentially reduce exploration costs. In most cases, geologic maps are readily available and should be reviewed so that the appropriate exploration techniques are implemented. Reliance on historical data for design (such as boring data, geologic maps) is not recommended unless supported by current exploration data.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 4 (Site Exploration), paragraph 4-3a, printed p. 66.

sections.title: Site reconnaissance
sections.body: [p. 67] Site reconnaissance. A site reconnaissance visit will help confirm findings from the data research phase and establish or guide exploration areas. Site observations should include topographical and (surface) geological characteristics of the site (such as surficial soils, rock outcrops), assessment of exploration access needs, surface and subsurface utility markings, site drainage, and apparent site modifications (such as partially exposed debris, cut, or fill slopes). Careful observation of damage to existing structures, such as cracks in buildings, could suggest foundation problems to be encountered or avoided.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 4 (Site Exploration), paragraph 4-3b, printed p. 67.

sections.title: Subsurface explorations
sections.body: [p. 67] Subsurface explorations. For shallow foundations, design parameters of primary concern include shear strength, compressibility, and those necessary to evaluate durability characteristics (such as pH, resistivity, chlorides), in addition to groundwater depths and presence of geologic hazards. Subsurface explorations are necessary to evaluate these conditions. A geotechnical engineer or geologist should be present during drilling activities to adjust sampling and testing (in situ or laboratory) requirements based on encountered conditions. Duties should include visual classification and description of geologic materials (such as hand penetrometer, torvane) and recording of field data.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 4 (Site Exploration), paragraph 4-3c, printed p. 67.

sections.title: Preliminary subsurface explorations
sections.body: [p. 67] Preliminary subsurface explorations.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 4 (Site Exploration), paragraph 4-3c(1), printed p. 67.

sections.title: The purpose of preliminary subsurface explorations is to obtain approximate …
sections.body: [p. 67] The purpose of preliminary subsurface explorations is to obtain approximate soil profiles and representative samples from principal strata or to broadly characterize bedrock or stratigraphic profiles by indirect methods. Auger or split-spoon borings are commonly used for obtaining representatives samples. Geophysical methods (such as shear wave velocity, electrical resistivity, refraction) are often used in preliminary exploration of sites for large projects; however, borings should be performed to verify correlations with geophysical data.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 4 (Site Exploration), paragraph 4-3c(1)(a), printed p. 67. The manual prints this subparagraph without a heading; the title is its opening words.

sections.title: Preliminary reconnaissance explorations furnish data for planning detailed and …
sections.body: [p. 67] Preliminary reconnaissance explorations furnish data for planning detailed and special exploration of sites for large and important projects. The preliminary exploration could be sufficient for some construction purposes associated with foundation design, such as excavation or borrow materials. It could also be adequate for foundation design of small warehouses, residential buildings, and retaining walls located in areas where soil properties have been reasonably well established.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 4 (Site Exploration), paragraph 4-3c(1)(b), printed p. 67. The manual prints this subparagraph without a heading; the title is its opening words.

sections.title: Detailed subsurface exploration
sections.body: [p. 67] Detailed subsurface exploration. For critical projects, complex subsurface conditions, and cases where preliminary subsurface explorations provide insufficient data for design, more detailed investigations should be performed. Detailed subsurface explorations are necessary to obtain more detailed geologic profiles, undisturbed samples, and cores for laboratory testing, or larger or more continuous representative samples of foundation materials. The amount of in situ or laboratory testing will vary depending on the availability of existing information, the subsurface characteristics, and the project requirements. Well-defined loading conditions should be established and referenced when determining the scope and extent of the investigation prior to implementing detailed subsurface exploration programs so that the appropriate foundation influence depths can be explored.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 4 (Site Exploration), paragraph 4-3c(2), printed p. 67.

sections.title: Exploration plan
sections.body: [p. 68] A field exploration plan should be approved by the district geotechnical design element. The plan should be developed through close cooperation between the project geologist and geotechnical engineer. Plans should identify known safety hazards (such as utility locations/markings), right of way or permits of entry requirements, access routes, property lines, instructions for limiting site impacts, exploration locations, and procedures to include minimum sample and testing intervals. Plans must be approved by the district Dam Safety Officer/Levee Safety Officer (DSO/LSO) if drilling into, in close proximity to, or through embankment dam and levees and their foundations (see ER 1110-1-1807).
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 4 (Site Exploration), paragraph 4-4, printed p. 68.

sections.title: Exploration methods and extent
sections.body: [p. 68] Numerous exploration methods are available for characterizing subsurface conditions and may be suitable. Exploration methods and their advantages/limitations are described in EM 1110-1-1804. For shallow foundation design, vertically drilled borings are generally necessary to efficiently sample, test, and characterize subsurface conditions. Minimum guidance for defining exploration extents, sample collection, testing intervals, and groundwater measurements is provided in paragraphs 4-5a through 4-8.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 4 (Site Exploration), paragraph 4-5, printed p. 68.

sections.title: Exploration location and spacing
sections.body: [p. 68] Exploration location and spacing. Reasonable locations for soil exploration (typically soil borings) should include, but not be limited to, near the center, edges, and corners of the proposed structure, and in potential borrow areas used to raise site grades above foundation areas. In certain cases, borings spaced at 40 ft or less could be necessary to adequately define erratic subsurface conditions (such as uncontrolled fill, lenses, boulders, bedrock irregularities).
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 4 (Site Exploration), paragraph 4-5a, printed p. 68.

sections.title: Exploration depth
sections.body: [p. 68] Exploration depth. Minimum exploration depths should account for changes in effective stress that can influence foundation settlements. For induced stresses, the depth of significant influence is described in paragraph 6-6c. Since foundation dimensions are not usually known in advance, exploration depths should reflect conservative assignments of foundation size based on anticipated or presumptive ground conditions. For determining seismic site classification and adjusting mapped spectral accelerations, the site should be classified based on the upper 100 ft of the site profile as permitted by code. sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 4 (Site Exploration), paragraph 4-5b, printed p. 68.

sections.title: Soft and loose soil deposits
sections.body: [p. 68] Soft and loose soil deposits. The thickness of soft and loose soils should be adequately determined (such as continuous or near-continuous sampling and testing) within the settlement zone of influence. Since the settlement zone of influence is not precisely known, borings are often extended some additional depth (to account for this uncertainty) or until more competent conditions are encountered.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 4 (Site Exploration), paragraph 4-5b(1), printed p. 68.

sections.title: Shallow refusal
sections.body: [p. 68] Shallow refusal. Depending on the drilling method, refusal at shallow depth can be an indicator of hard or dense zones (such as shallow rock, cobbles/boulders, buried [p. 69] debris). Where these conditions are encountered (or suspected), offset borings and other exploratory methods (such as test pits, rock coring, geophysics) are recommended to better characterize the subsurface conditions.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 4 (Site Exploration), paragraph 4-5b(2), printed pp. 68 to 69.

sections.title: Depth to primary formation
sections.body: [p. 69] Depth to primary formation. Typically, depth of exploration need not exceed the depth of the primary formation where rock or soil of exceptional bearing capacity and compressibility characteristics is located.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 4 (Site Exploration), paragraph 4-5b(3), printed p. 69.

sections.title: In situ test intervals
sections.body: [p. 69] In situ tests should be performed at significant changes in soil strata (such as stress state, soil type). Minimum in situ test intervals are predicated on standard test methods (ASTM) and are described in paragraph 4-10; however, larger intervals may be adequate. For SPT methods, test intervals should not exceed 2.5 ft in the upper 10 ft and 5 ft thereafter within foundation influence depths.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 4 (Site Exploration), paragraph 4-6, printed p. 69.

sections.title: Soil sampling
sections.body: [p. 69] Soil samples should be obtained at significant changes in soil strata (such as stress state, soil type). Commonly, thin-walled tube and disturbed samples are obtained during field exploration activities associated with shallow foundations; however, alternate sampling techniques (such as undisturbed block, ASTM D7015) may also be used. Table 4-1 and Table 4-2 may be used as a guide for determining the required sizes of thin-walled tube and disturbed samples, respectively. Sampling methods should adhere to standard practices (ASTM) to include preserving, storage, and transporting. In general, intact samples of clean sands and gravels cannot be obtained using conventional sampling methods. For this reason, in situ testing methods are commonly used in these soils.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 4 (Site Exploration), paragraph 4-7, printed p. 69.

sections.title: Thin-walled tube samples
sections.body: [p. 69] Thin-walled tube samples. Thin-walled tube soil samplers are described in EM 1110-1-1804. Sampling of cohesive soils should be according to ASTM D1587. Strength index tests (such as lab vane) and visual observation should be performed above and below cohesive specimens obtained from thin-walled tubes to assess relative changes in sample quality. It may not be possible to obtain samples of very soft or hard soils using a thin-walled tube sampler. For these cases, in situ testing methods may be necessary for engineering evaluation.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 4 (Site Exploration), paragraph 4-7a, printed p. 69.

sections.title: Sample disturbance
sections.body: [p. 69] Sample disturbance. Thin-walled tube sampling results in a stress change, possible pore water change, and some structure alteration because of displacement effects of the sampler. Sample disturbance is influenced by sampling method, transportation, storage, and trimming. Practices for preserving and transporting soil samples to reduce disturbance should be adhered, reference ASTM D4220. The effects of sampling disturbance on laboratory-measured soil properties are detailed in Miscellaneous Paper (MP) GL-92-35 (U.S. Army Engineer Waterways Experiment Station). Sample disturbance can generally be evaluated using the following methods; however, no definitive method exists to determine the absolute sample quality.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 4 (Site Exploration), paragraph 4-7a(1), printed p. 69.

sections.title: Area ratio and inside clearance ratio
sections.body:
[p. 70] Area ratio and inside clearance ratio. Sample disturbance is related to the area ratio (Ar) as defined in equation 4-1 and to the inside clearance ratio (ICR), as defined in equation 4-2. For an acceptable degree of disturbance, the ICR should be approximately 1 percent and the area ratio should 10 percent or less. Thin-walled tubes are typically manufactured to meet these specifications, but a thicker-walled tube with an ICR of zero is commonly used in the Gulf states (Texas, Louisiana) to sample very stiff, overconsolidated clays. The thicker-walled tube is intended to minimize buckling of the sampler in the stiff deposits, and the ICR of zero criteria is intended to minimize sample expansion within the tube.

Ar = ((Do^2 − Di^2)/Di^2) x 100% [Eq. 4-1]

ICR = (Di − De)/De [Eq. 4-2]

where:
Ar = area ratio (dimensionless)
ICR = inside clearance ratio (percent)
Do = outside diameter of sampler tube (in)
Di = inside diameter of the cutting shoe (in)
De = diameter of the sampler cutting tip (in)

sections.title: Recovery ratio
sections.body:
[p. 70] Recovery ratio. Sample quality is indicated by recovery ratio (Lr) defined in equation 4-3. A value of Lr < 1 indicates that the sample was compressed or lost during recovery, and Lr >1 indicates the sample expanded during recovery or excess soil was forced into the sampler. Undisturbed samples should be handled and stored to preserve stratification or structure, water content, and in situ stresses.

Recovery Ratio, Lr = (Length of recovered sample, in)/(Length of sample tube pushed, in) [Eq. 4-3]

sections.title: Sample quality
sections.body:
[p. 71] Sample quality. Sample quality can be estimated from Table 4-2 by obtaining the vertical strain obtained from a standard oedometer test at a vertical pressure equal to the in situ vertical effective stress (σ′vo) calculated for the appropriate field conditions. A sample quality designation (SQD) of 4 percent means that the oedometer sample strained 4 percent upon reaching a vertical stress that is equal to σ′vo (the sample expanded about 4 percent upon extraction). Effects of sample disturbance on a consolidation test e-log-p curve are illustrated in for an OC clay. Practically, no soil sample can be obtained in a perfectly undisturbed state. The sample quality designation (SQD) should be rated as very good to excellent for use in strength evaluation or consolidation characteristics.

sections.title: Disturbed samples
sections.body:
[p. 72] Disturbed samples. Disturbed soil samples, which alter the macro-structure of the soil, can be obtained by various methods (such as auger or mechanically pushed, or driven sampling). Thick-wall, solid, or split-barrel drive samplers can be used in most soils, excluding gravelly soils. Samples obtained with a drive sampler should be not less than 2 inches, and preferably 3 inches or more in diameter. Where loose sands or soft silts are encountered, a special sampler with a flap valve or a plunger should be used to hold the material in the barrel. The minimum recommended sample size for a disturbed sample is provided in Table 4-3.

sections.title: Groundwater measurements
sections.body: [p. 72] Groundwater levels should be obtained in boreholes during drilling to document groundwater levels for shallow foundation design and constructability purposes. Groundwater conditions can be complex due to artesian conditions, perched groundwater, and interbedded aquicludes and aquifers. Due to the low permeability of fine-grained soils, a long period of time may be required for water levels to stabilize. For low-permeability soils, water levels should be obtained after a period approximately 24 hours after drilling is completed. Instrumentation (typically monitoring wells or piezometers) should be installed to monitor groundwater levels if potential borehole collapse or “cave-in” could occur. Where groundwater levels are influenced by nearby water bodies (ocean, river), historical water level data should be reviewed and could influence design.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 4 (Site Exploration), paragraph 4-8, printed p. 72.

sections.title: Observation wells
sections.body: [p. 72] Observation wells. Observation (or monitoring) wells consist of vertical pipes with a slotted section at the bottom or a tube with a porous tip at the bottom (Figure 4-2a). Observation wells are appropriate in relatively uniform, pervious material. Often, the top of the borehole is sealed to prevent surface water from entering the borehole. Observation wells create a hydraulic connection between strata and could lead to misinterpreted groundwater conditions.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 4 (Site Exploration), paragraph 4-8a, printed p. 72.

sections.title: Piezometers
sections.body:
[p. 73] Piezometers. Piezometers consist of a vertical pipe with a screened (or measured) interval (Figure 4-2b). Seals are usually placed as bentonite clay or cement grout. Pipe joints should be watertight to prevent leakage. Various types of piezometers can be installed; however, open standpipes (observation wells with subsurface seals) are more common.

sections.title: Borehole closure
sections.body: [p. 73] Borings should be backfilled after completion of field activities. Backfilling should be performed by tremie grouting through drilling rods or other pipes. Backfilling should be performed according to state and environmental regulations.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 4 (Site Exploration), paragraph 4-9, printed p. 73.

sections.title: In situ testing
sections.body:
[p. 73] Appropriate in situ testing methods should be assigned, see EM 1110-1-1804. Commonly, borehole penetration tests (such as SPT, CPT) and deformation tests (such as DMT, PMT, VST) are used to characterize subsurface conditions for shallow foundation design. See Table 4-4. In some cases, depending on equipment or test limitations, several methods may be necessary to adequately define subsurface conditions. However, direct comparison between different in situ or laboratory tests can be misleading due to different modes of deformation. For estimating foundation settlement, borehole deformation tests (such as DMT, PMT) are recommended due to [p. 74] strain rate effects associated with penetration tests. For gravelly sites, reference EM 1110-1-1804 for guidance on in situ testing methods.

sections.title: Standard penetration test
sections.body: [p. 74] Standard penetration test.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 4 (Site Exploration), paragraph 4-10a, printed p. 74.

sections.title: Application
sections.body: [p. 74] Application. The SPT is an in situ penetration test described in ASTM D1586. Disturbed “split-spoon” samples (1.5-ft to 2-ft length) can be obtained during testing, continuously or intermittently. In general, SPT blow count data are most useful for fine-grained sands, with coarser sands and silty sands giving reasonably useful results. For gravelly and fine-grained soils, SPT can be unreliable for obtaining strength or stiffness properties. Engineering behavior of saturated or nearly saturated silty sands could be underestimated by the SPT. A typical production rate is 120 lineal feet per shift.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 4 (Site Exploration), paragraph 4-10a(1), printed p. 74.

sections.title: Standard penetration test N-value corrections
sections.body: [p. 75] Standard penetration test N-value corrections. Several factors contribute to variations of the standard penetration test (SPT) N-value at a given depth for similar soil profiles. These include SPT hammer efficiency, borehole diameter, sampling method, rod length, water table, and overburden pressure. Schmertmann et al. (1978) and Kovacs and Salomone (1982) identify the most significant factors affecting measured N-values as (1) the amount of energy delivered to the drill rods, and (2) the method used to drill and support the borehole. The engineer should be familiar with the N-value requirements of the correlations or direct design methods.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 4 (Site Exploration), paragraph 4-10a(2), printed p. 75.

sections.title: Field procedures and hammer efficiency
sections.body:
[p. 75] Field procedures and hammer efficiency. SPT design correlations were popularized circa 1950 and are widely used today; however, testing methods have been modernized. N-value corrections allow these established correlations to remain valid and standardize drilling procedures. The measured SPT N-value is typically adjusted for hammer efficiency per equation 4-4a. Additional correction factors may also be needed to arrive at a more standardized value of N60 per equation 4-4b. The corrections are applicable for both cohesive and cohesionless soils. Hammer efficiency should be verified using the methods of ASTM D4633; typical energy correction factors are provided in Table 4-5.

N60 = Nm · ETR/60 [Eq. 4-4a]

N60 = Nm · CE · CB · CR · CS [Eq. 4-4b]

where:
N60 = standard penetration resistance adjusted to a 60% drill rod energy ratio (blows/ft); note: may also be corrected for field procedures
ETR = ratio of the measured energy transferred to the drill rods to the theoretical energy per ASTM D4633; the ratio ETR/60 is also referred to as an energy ratio, (CE) in equation 4-4b and Table 4-5.
CB, CR, CS = field procedure correction factors, see Table 4-6 (dimensionless)
Nm = measured SPT N-value in field (blows/foot) per ASTM D1586

sections.body:
[p. 76] Overburden stress correction. In cohesionless soils, SPT N-values are affected by the effective overburden stress, and therefore, an overburden correction factor (CN) is recommended per equation 4-5 (Liao and Whitman 1985). For cohesive soils, there is no need for overburden pressure correction (Peck et al. 1974).

(N1)60 = penetration resistance, N60 normalized to a 1 ton/ft^2 stress level (blows/ft)

N60 = corrected SPT N-value per equation 4-4 (blows/ft)
Pa = atmospheric pressure; at sea level Pa ≈ 2,116 psf (101.3 kPa)

sections.title: Correction of standard penetration test N-value for water table
sections.body:
[p. 77] Correction of standard penetration test N-value for water table. For dense or very dense fine sand and silt below the water table, dilatancy effects can influence SPT N-values, resulting in abnormally high SPT N-values. For penetration resistance, (N1)60 greater than 15 blows per foot (bpf), equation 4-7 (Terzaghi and Peck 1967) may be used to correct for dilatancy effects. For coarse sand, this correction is not applicable. In applying this correction, overburden correction should be applied first and then corrected for dilatancy.

(N1)60(corr) = 15 + (1/2)[(N1)60 − 15] [Eq. 4-7]

where:
(N1)60(corr) = corrected (N1)60 value for dilatancy/water table effects (blows/ft)
(N1)60 = penetration resistance, N60 normalized to a 1 ton/ft^2 stress level (blows/ft)

sections.title: Gravel in the soil matrix
sections.body:
[p. 77] Gravel in the soil matrix. In 1987, Andrus and Youd (see MP GL-87-8) describe an alternate procedure for determining SPT N-Values in gravel. They suggest that the penetration per blow be measured and the cumulative penetration versus blow be plotted, reference Figure 4-3. With this procedure, changes in slope could be identified when gravel particles interfere with penetration.

Figure 4-3. Examples of interpreting standard penetration test blow counts on a per-inch basis: (a) smooth driving patterns that do not require corrections to N-values and (b) strong increases in driving resistance that, along with sample recoveries, suggest that the sampler encountered large particles; this graph also shows the adjusted N-value, based on extrapolating the pre-obstruction driving rate

sections.title: Cone penetration test
sections.body: [p. 78] Cone penetration test. The CPT, ASTM D3441 and ASTM D5778, is a quasi-static penetration test. Test results are usually obtained at 1-inch to 2-inch depth intervals for estimating soil properties. The CPT is generally suitable in soft to medium dense sand, silt, and clay, and is not generally suitable in glacially overconsolidated soil, rock, and gravel or debris. For penetration of very dense and hard soils, pre-drilling or advancement through hollow stem augers may be necessary. Although not typical, discrete soil samples can be obtained using piston-type samplers that typically measure 12-inch length by 1-inch diameter. A typical production rate is 400 lineal feet per shift. Other applications include measurement of shear wave velocity (with a seismic module), and inclination or verticality measurements.

sections.title: Piezocone penetration test
sections.body: [p. 78] Piezocone penetration test.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 4 (Site Exploration), paragraph 4-10b(1), printed p. 78.

sections.title: Application
sections.body: [p. 78] Application. The Piezocone penetration test (CPTu) is a cone penetration test with pore water pressure measurements. Between one and three pore pressure sensors can be used. The pore pressure measurements help to better distinguish between sands and clays and can be used for determining deformation and permeability characteristics. The rate of penetration for the CPTu test is the same as the basic CPT test unless pore water dissipation testing is performed.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 4 (Site Exploration), paragraph 4-10b(1)(a), printed p. 78.

sections.title: Pore water dissipation tests
sections.body:
[p. 78] Pore water dissipation tests. Dissipation tests measure the decay of pore water pressure over time in saturated soil. During a dissipation test, the CPTu is paused at specified intervals, and pore water pressure decay readings are recorded in situ. The test is usually performed until a time at which 50 percent of the pore water has dissipated (t50) to assess hydraulic conductivity and coefficient of consolidation. If conditions are hydrostatic, the equilibrium water pressure (uo) can be used to calculate the approximate depth of the ground water table. The water table (or phreatic surface) depth is defined as the distance below the soil surface at which pore pressure is equal to atmospheric pressure, per equation 4-8. The water head (hw) is the height of the water above the cone, per equation 4-9.

dwater = dcone − hw [Eq. 4-8]

where:
dwater = depth of water table (ft)
dcone = depth of piezocone (ft)
hw = water head (ft)

hw = uo/γw + z [Eq. 4-9]

where:
hw = water head (ft)
uo = equilibrium pore pressure determined from dissipation test (psf)
γw = unit weight of water (pcf)
z = distance, if any, between pressure sensor location and depth reference point on the piezocone (ft)

sections.body: [p. 79] Measured and interpreted parameters. Numerous correlations have been developed to estimate soil parameters from CPT data. Common measured and interpreted parameters used in these correlations are shown in Table 4-7.

sections.title: Soil behavior type
sections.body:
[p. 79] Soil behavior type. The primary parameters for soil behavior type (SBT) are: (1) cone resistance (qc, qt, or Qt), (2) friction ratio (Rf), and (3) pore water measurements (commonly measured at the u2 position). SBT is categorized in Figure 4-4 and Table 4-8. Figure 4-4 depicts the shifts in SBTs based on adjustments when introducing pore pressure measurements and normalizing cone resistance. Other charts by Schmertmann (1978), Douglas and Olsen (1981), Robertson (1990), and Schneider et al. (2008) may also be used for evaluating soil type. Although SBT charts can be similar in appearance and results, each has its own limitations.

sections.title: Flat plate dilatometer test
sections.body: [p. 80] Flat plate dilatometer test.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 4 (Site Exploration), paragraph 4-10c, printed p. 80.

sections.title: Application
sections.body: [p. 80] Application. The dilatometer test (ASTM D6635) is a calibrated, static deformation test that can be used to estimate soil parameters and provide information [p. 81] on stress history. It is generally not suitable for testing gravel, hard rock, or soils with angular gravel size stone which can damage the membrane; however, it is commonly used in residual soils (SPT N < 30 bpf), which can be hard to penetrate.

sections.title: Testing and sampling
sections.body:
[p. 81] Testing and sampling. The DMT has a wedge-shaped tip for reduced soil disturbance (Figure 4-5). Testing is specified at approximate 8- to 12-inch increments (1 to 2 minutes per test) and the thrust pressure applied for advancement can be recorded to aid in soil characterization. A typical production rate (at ~8-inch intervals) is 400 feet per day per shift. Although not typical, it is possible to take small-diameter samples using the same pushing equipment used to insert the probe. Shear wave velocity measurements can also be obtained where a seismic module is incorporated (SDMT).

The A, B, and C readings are corrected during calibration to account for membrane stiffness, pressure gage zero offset, and other factors using equipment calibration readings per equations 4-10 through 4-12 (Marchetti 1999).

sections.title: Intermediate dilatometer parameters
sections.body:
[p. 82] Intermediate dilatometer parameters. Four “intermediate” parameters are interpreted from the corrected DMT measurements, reference equations 4-13 through 4-16. The DMT modulus (ED) is an uncorrected and intermediate parameter and should be converted to the constrained modulus (MDMT) for use in settlement evaluations, reference paragraph 3-9c(2). The material index (ID) is based on mechanical response without benefit of grain size distribution; however, it can be used to help estimate soil stratigraphy and soil type. Similarly, the pore water pressure index (UD) can be used as an indicator of soil type as well as to correlate other soil parameters with DMT data (such as soil unit weight).

Material Index, ID = (p1 − po)/(po − uo) [Eq. 4-13]

Horizontal Stress Index, KD = (po − uo)/σ′vo [Eq. 4-14]

Dilatometer Modulus, ED = 34.7 (p1 − po) [Eq. 4-15]

UD = pore water pressure index (dimensionless); in free-draining soils, p2 ≈ uo, UD ≈ 1. In non-free draining soils, p2 will be higher than uo and UD.

sections.title: Dilatometer dissipation test
sections.body:
[p. 83] Dilatometer dissipation test. Dissipation tests are not feasible in relatively permeable soils (such as silty sands). In clean sands, excess pore pressures are not generated during penetration of the DMT; however, in soft clays, the basic DMT data (po, p1) are dominated by large penetration pore pressures (Campanella et al. 1985). The coefficient of consolidation in the horizontal direction (Ch) can be estimated from dissipation tests using various methods, reference ASTM D6635. The DMT-A method (Marchetti and Totani 1989) utilizes the A-reading and is generally preferred. Other methods include the DMT-C method and the DMT-A2 method. An example plot is shown in Figure 4-6.

Figure 4-6. Example of dissipation test in cohesive soils, dilatometer test-A method (Totani and Monaco 1998)

sections.title: Soil classification
sections.body: [p. 83] Soil classification. Soil behavioral response from DMT can be used to evaluate soil classification. A general relationship between material index (ID), DMT modulus (ED), and soil type is shown in Figure 4-7. Another general indicator of soil type is the [p. 84] pore pressure index (UD). Typically, coarse-grained (such as clean sands and gravels) will exhibit a UD between 0.0 and 0.2. Fine-grained soils (such as lean and fat clays, elastic silts) will exhibit a UD of 0.7 or greater. A wide range of soils can have an intermediate permeability that exhibit UD between 0.2 and 0.7. UD values are a general indication of soil type and should be used in conjunction with ID to characterize soil type.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 4 (Site Exploration), paragraph 4-10c(6), printed pp. 83 to 84.

sections.title: Pressuremeter test
sections.body: [p. 84] Pressuremeter test. Pressuremeter tests (PMTs) can be used to estimate the stress-strain response in a wide variety of soils and soft/weak rock. In cohesive soils, the PMT can be used to determine both the immediate and consolidation settlements together. Various types of pressuremeters are available (such as pre-bored, self-boring). Standard test methods for the pre-bored PMT are described in ASTM D4719 and consist of drilling a borehole, removing the drilling tool, and lowering the probe in the open borehole (Figure 4-8). Probe diameters are in the range of 2 to 3 inches, and the length of the inflatable part of the probe is in the range of 12 to 24 inches. Minimum spacing between consecutive tests (probe center to center) should not be less than 1.5 times the length of the inflatable part of the probe. For pre-bored methods, borehole disturbance in very soft clays and very loose sands can be significant. Production rate for PMT testing is typically 2 to 6 tests per shift.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 4 (Site Exploration), paragraph 4-10d, printed p. 84.

sections.title: Interpretation of pressuremeter test results
sections.body:
[p. 84] Interpretation of pressuremeter test results. During testing, a pressuremeter modulus and a limit pressure are obtained. Three characteristic segments of a pre-bored PMT pressure-volume change plot are illustrated in Figure 4-9 and include: (1) the re-loading phase; (2) the pseudo-elastic phase; and (3) the plastic phase. After the borehole is drilled and the augers are withdrawn, the borehole walls relax, and the cavity volume is reduced. As the pressuremeter probe is initially inflated, the walls of the borehole are pushed back to their original position. The point at which the volume of the borehole cavity has fully returned to its initial position corresponds to the in situ horizontal stress is given the coordinates, Vo, po. The pseudo-elastic phase is similar to the elastic behavior of steel or concrete. The plastic phase begins once the creep pressure has been reached, and which corresponds with coordinates, Vf, Pf. During the plastic phase, the data plots asymptotic to the limit pressure (Pl). The limit pressure is defined as the pressure reached for the infinite expansion of the cylinder.

sections.title: Pressuremeter modulus
sections.body:
[p. 87] Pressuremeter modulus. The pressuremeter modulus, Eo (also denoted Ep) is calculated over the pseudo-elastic range per ASTM D4719 and equation 4-17. Designing beyond the yield pressure (Py) is not recommended. If it needs to be done, then the modulus used should be a secant modulus related to the line joining the beginning of the straight line in the PMT curve to the point corresponding to the pressure applied in the geotechnical problem. Harder and denser soils will have a higher PMT modulus, having a flatter pressure vs. volume curve. The pressuremeter modulus has been related empirically to the elastic modulus of the soil as E0/E = α, (Ménard 1965), in which α is termed by Ménard as the rheological coefficient and has a value between 0 and 1, reference Table 7-6.

Pressuremeter Modulus, Eo = 2(1 + υ)(Vo + Vm) ΔP/ΔV [Eq. 4-17]

Note. The PMT provides a measure of the horizontal modulus in soils. In clays, the pressuremeter modulus is approximately equal to the undrained elastic modulus (Kulhawy and Mayne 1990). The “undrained” PMT modulus value obtained in fine-grained soils has been compared to case histories and load tests and typically gives the long-term settlement.[1]

sections.title: Initial total horizontal pressure, Po
sections.body:
[p. 87] Initial total horizontal pressure, Po. For the pre-bored PMT, the pressure at the beginning of the pseudo-elastic phase (Po) is often interpreted as the in situ horizontal stress (σho). As shown in Figure 4-9, the initial expansion of the probe mobilizes a low resistance in seating the membrane to the soil and deforming a disturbed annular zone of the soil. Upon further expansion, the resistance increases, and the curve becomes somewhat flatter. The point where the curve becomes relatively linear can be interpreted as an approximate representation of σho as the probe has reapplied the

sections.title: Limit pressure, PL
sections.body: [p. 88] Limit pressure, PL. The limit pressure is defined as the pressure reached for the infinite expansion of the cylinder (FHWA-IP-89-008). This is the point where no additional pressure is required to continue to apply strain to the soil (see Figure 4-9). The conventional limit pressure (PL) is defined as the pressure where the probe volume reaches twice the original soil volume cavity volume, defined as 2Vo + Vi, where Vi is the corrected volume reading at the pressure where the probe contacted the borehole. The limit pressure is usually not obtained by direct measurement due to limitation of probe expansion or excessively high pressure. If the volumetric increase at the end of the test is less than twice the cavity volume, extrapolation can be used to calculate PL. Common values of the pressuremeter modulus and net limit pressure are summarized in Table 4-10.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 4 (Site Exploration), paragraph 4-10d(1)(c), printed p. 88.

sections.title: Net limit pressure, P*L
sections.body:
[p. 88] Net limit pressure, P*L. The net limit pressure is used for calculating bearing capacity and can be calculated using equation 4-18. Although the initial horizontal pressure (Po) should equal the pressure corresponding to the volume required to inflate the pressuremeter and push soil to its original position (vo), it is difficult to accurately establish Po from the test data due to disturbance of the borehole walls and a lack of points at the beginning of the test.

Net Limit Pressure, P*L = PL − Po [Eq. 4-18]

where:
P*L = net limit pressure (tsf)
PL = limit pressure (tsf)
Po = initial total horizontal pressure in the ground (tsf) = [(γm − u)z]Ko + u
γm = moist unit weight of soil above test interval (tsf)
u = pore water pressure at test interval (tsf)
z = depth to middle of test probe below ground surface (ft)
Ko = at-rest lateral earth pressure coefficient

sections.title: Yield pressure, Py
sections.body: [p. 88] Yield pressure, Py. The yield pressure (Py), also referred to as creep pressure (Pf), is found at the end of the straight line corresponding to the PMT modulus and is comparable to the preconsolidation pressure. Typically, Py is 0.5PL for clays and 0.33PL for sands (Briaud 2013). At working loads, it is advisable to keep the pressure under these limits to avoid creep deformations. Designing beyond the yield pressure is not recommended.

sections.title: Soil type based on pressuremeter data
sections.body:
[p. 88] Soil type based on pressuremeter data. Soil type can be classified from soil samples obtained during drilling. Soil type can also be characterized by observing the soil cuttings and the general shape of the corrected pressuremeter curve as illustrated in Figure 4-10, and the ratio of the pressuremeter modulus (E0), to the net limit pressure (P*L), per equations 4-19 and 4-20.

sections.title: Pressuremeter holding test
sections.body:
[p. 89] Pressuremeter holding test. The pressuremeter holding test can be used to determine creep and consolidation characteristics of clays. During a PMT holding test, either the pressure or strain is held constant over a period during which pore water dissipation occurs. If the total pressure is held constant, it will expand (as the cavity diameter increases) and the excess pore pressures dissipate. Alternatively, the maximum strain (~10 percent) can be held constant, in what is known as the strain hold test (SHT) (Clarke et al. 1979). Holding the expansion of the probe constant is similar to a piezocone dissipation test and can be analyzed in the same manner. During the strain hold test, relaxation of the soil is observed by the decrease of measured excess pore pressure and total cavity pressure. An example holding test is shown in Figure 4-11.

sections.title: Field vane shear test
sections.body: [p. 90] Field vane shear test.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 4 (Site Exploration), paragraph 4-10e, printed p. 90.

sections.title: Application
sections.body: [p. 90] Application. Field vane shear testing (FVST) (ASTM D2573) is performed to evaluate the in situ undrained shear strength of fine-grained, cohesive soil. The apparatus consists of four blades on the end of a rod as shown in Figure 4-12 and Figure 4-13. VST is well suited for very soft to firm clays; however, is not applicable in sandy soils or non-plastic silts as these can allow drainage during testing. The presence of gravels can cause the results to be too high, and therefore, should be verified using other means (such as SHANSEP comparisons or other in situ or laboratory testing methods).
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 4 (Site Exploration), paragraph 4-10e(1), printed p. 90.

sections.title: Companion tests
sections.body: [p. 90] Companion tests. The test is often performed in conjunction with SPT borings (or in companion borings to SPT borings), CPTs (such as to validate the cone factors), DMTs, and PMTs. Tests intervals should be assigned once the stratigraphy is characterized. The VST may be performed either at the bottom of a prebored hole or, in soft clays, by merely pushing the vane rods to the desired test depth. The latter requires a correction for rod friction.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 4 (Site Exploration), paragraph 4-10e(2), printed p. 90.

sections.title: Test pits and trenches
sections.body: [p. 90] Test pits and trenches. Test pits and trench excavations can allow visual inspection of subsurface conditions and can be advantageous in some cases (such as shallow testing/sampling, delineation of uncontrolled fills, colluvium, and shallow rock). Excavators can typically be used to excavate test pits or trenches to depths up to about 10 to 20 ft; however, dewatering could be required. In some cases, exploratory trench excavations can be used in fault evaluation studies. An extension of a rock fault into much younger overburden materials exposed by trenching is usually considered proof [p. 91] of recent fault activity. Consult Occupational Health and Safety Administration (OSHA) guidelines on trenching/shoring.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 4 (Site Exploration), paragraph 4-10f, printed pp. 90 to 91.

sections.title: Geophysical methods
sections.body:
[p. 91] Geophysical methods. Geophysical methods may be used to characterize subsurface conditions between borings. Common geophysical methods for use in shallow foundation design include measurement or estimation of shear wave (S-wave) velocity, seismic refraction (P-wave), electrical resistivity, and ground penetrating radar. Geophysical data should be used in conjunction with boring/penetration tests and interpreted by qualified experienced personnel. Geophysical methods are further discussed in EM 1110-1-1804.

sections.title: Laboratory testing
sections.body: [p. 92] Laboratory testing should be performed to establish engineering characteristics. Guidance for recommended testing procedures for making determinations of the soil properties to be used in design is provided in EM 1110-2-1906. Laboratory testing is generally necessary to verify visual classification of soil samples, for estimating or comparing strength and settlement parameters with in situ test data, and for determining corrosion characteristics (such as sulfate, sulfides). Depending on the subsurface conditions encountered, laboratory testing could range from simple laboratory index tests to performance tests (such as those used to characterize soil strength and compressibility). Laboratories performing geotechnical testing must be validated to comply with ER 11101-8100.
